tagline.text: Davao's month-long August thanksgiving festival of Indigenous cultures and flower floats

location.text: Magsaysay Park and City Hall area, Davao City

children.text: Kadayawan is the Philippines' best-known thanksgiving festival, held every August in Davao City to celebrate the cultures of 11 Indigenous communities and the joy of the harvest. Its climax is the flower float parade and street dance competition on the final big weekend.
The Kadayawan Festival is a thanksgiving celebration held in August in Davao City, in southern Mindanao. The name comes from the Mandaya word
madayaw

, understood to mean "good, valuable, superior or beautiful." According to the city, it is a time to give thanks for the gifts of nature, culture, the harvest and a peaceful life. Filipinos call it a "festival of festivals" because of its scale, and like Sinulog or MassKara it gives you the feeling of an entire city caught up in the celebration. The flower float parade is said to be modeled on the Rose Parade in Pasadena, California, so floats decorated with flowers and fruit close out the festival.

Its roots go back to the 1970s. It is said to have begun in 1970 when Mayor Elias Lopez encouraged Davao's tribes to present their own harvest thanksgiving rituals. In the mid-1980s it was held as "Apo Duwaling," named for Mount Apo, the durian and the waling-waling orchid, and in 1988 it was renamed "Kadayawan sa Dabaw," the name it carries today. Those three emblems are still the faces of Davao. During the COVID-19 years of 2020–2021 it was held mostly online, and street events have since returned.

The stars of the festival are the 11 ethnolinguistic communities recognized by Davao City: the Ata, Bagobo-Klata, Bagobo-Tagabawa, Iranun, Kagan, Maguindanaon, Maranao, Matigsalug, Obu Manuvu, Sama and Tausug. The deputy mayor representing each community strikes the gong at the opening, and in 2026 all 11 deputy mayors did so. That is why Kadayawan is less a simple parade than a cultural trip in which Christian, Muslim and Indigenous traditions come together in one city. In 2026 the city also gave each of the 11 communities ₱700,000 to repair tribal houses and take part in the festival, so visiting the tribal village is also a way of supporting this culture.

It runs all month, but the schedule is not packed. In 2026 there were 26 official events: the festival opened on August 7 and closed on August 16 with the flower float parade and street dance showdown, while some events, such as the projection show on City Hall, continued until August 31. The city said it expected about 250,000 visitors in 2026, after 206,506 in 2025. Dates change every year, so please check the latest Davao City tourism announcements before you go. Security is also heavy: in 2026 about 19,000 police and security personnel were deployed, and the festival is reported to have ended without major incidents.

It is held early in the morning on the final day, usually the third Sunday of the month. Floats decorated with flowers and fruit (Pamulak) and street dance troupes in Indigenous costumes (Indak-Indak) march from
Roxas Avenue toward San Pedro Square
. In 2026 it started on August 16 at
. You watch from the roadside, so it is easy to join in. Each troupe has different props, chants and drumbeats, so it never gets dull however long you watch.

This is the final stage where the dance troupes that marched compete. In 2026 it was held for the first time on the Davao Coastal Road (near Tulip Drive), and about 120,000 people are reported to have turned out. It is divided into an open category and a school-based category, with prize money at stake.

During the festival, traditional houses and performance spaces for each community are set up in the park. In front of the houses you can browse crafts, textiles and beadwork and taste traditional food. In 2025 the festival opened on August 8 after the tribal houses were repaired, and in 2026 the opening ceremony on August 7 was held here. With the houses of all 11 communities in one place, the biggest appeal is being able to compare several cultures in a single day.

This is a selection event for women representing each community; the 2026 Grand Coronation was on August 13. It is closer to a showcase of traditional knowledge and cultural understanding than a beauty pageant.

blocks.title: Agong ug Kulintangan and Dula Kadayawan

children.text: The agong is a gong and the kulintang is a traditional Mindanao instrument played on a row of eight gongs. In 2026, Agong ug Kulintangan took place on August 14, and Dula Kadayawan (a folk performance) and a concert on August 15. They build the mood the day before the grand parade.

August is durian season, and the Kadayawan Durian Festival at SM Lanang continued into early September in 2026. Food bazaars appear around the city, and tropical fruits such as pomelo, mangosteen and marang are easy to find.

In 2026 a video projection show on the Davao City Hall building ran until August 31. It is a good evening stroll away from the daytime heat. At the same time, malls around the city hold Kadayawan food bazaars and markets, so you can also pick up light snacks and souvenirs.

blocks.title: Dayaw arts and film festival and smaller events

children.text: In 2026 there was Dayaw, an arts, culture and film festival, from August 8 to 15, a short film competition and the Tunog Kadayawan songwriting competition on August 8, and Bantawan, a showcase of traditional food, from August 10 to 12. Beyond the big parades, there are many chances to look quietly into the culture.
Leave your hotel early and head toward Roxas Avenue. Roads are closed, so be ready to walk about
1–2 km
, and bring only a small pouch and a clear water bottle.

The flower floats and Indak-Indak parade begin. The best time for photos is before the sun gets high. Floats and dance troupes pass one after another, so once you find a spot you can watch for a long time.
After the parade, have lunch in the city and rest at your hotel or a mall to escape the heat.
If you plan to watch the Grand Showdown, check the location in advance and head over. The venue is very crowded.
Have dinner at Davao Global Township or a restaurant in the city. If the City Hall projection show is on that night, stop by.

items.title: 2–3 day plan
items.subtitle: Festival weekend and day trips from Davao

children.text: Arrive in the afternoon, look around the tribal village at Magsaysay Park, and have dinner at a food bazaar. After sunset the heat fades and walking is more comfortable.
Walk around San Pedro Cathedral and downtown in the morning, then watch performances and a concert in the afternoon. If the City Hall projection mapping is on, stop by in the evening.
Watch the grand parade, then after lunch take a half-day trip to
Eden Nature Park
or
Samal Island
Event dates change every year, so it is safest to book flights and lodging after the official schedule comes out (usually in July).
A direct flight from Manila (NAIA) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO) takes about
2 hours
(roughly 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours 10 minutes depending on the airline and flight; nonstop on Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific).
Flights and rooms sell out quickly during festival week, so it is best to book as soon as the schedule is announced.
Fares vary widely by season and airline, so check booking sites.
Check booking sites to see whether flights to Davao operate from Cebu and other cities. Routes and operations vary by season.

items.title: From the airport to the city

children.text: Many people take a taxi or Grab from the airport to the city, and travel time varies a lot with road conditions.
Roads are jammed on parade day, so it is safer to stay in the city the day before.
Roads around the parade route are closed and parked cars are towed, so walk or take a jeepney only as close as you can get.
Get on and off Grab and taxis outside the closed area.

The festival lasts all of August, but the best time is the third Friday-to-Sunday stretch known as the "Great Kadayawan Weekend." In 2026 that was August 14–16, and August 14 was declared a special non-working holiday in Davao City.
Davao sits relatively outside the typhoon belt, so the weather in August tends to be stable. Showers can still arrive suddenly, so bring a raincoat and a light hat.

Less crowded than parade week, so you can enjoy the traditional houses and performances at a relaxed pace.

The Hiyas coronation, performances and the grand parade follow one another, and it is the most crowded time.
Food bazaars, durian events and the City Hall video show are still running.

The most convenient place to stay is in Davao City itself. The city's 2026 guide also pointed to downtown hotels such as DusitD2 Davao, Waterfront Insular Hotel Davao, Acacia Hotel Davao and The Royal Mandaya Hotel. Rooms fill up early on festival weekends, so book first. The parade route (Roxas Avenue to San Pedro Square) is in the city center, so staying near it makes movement easier even at dawn. If you cannot get a room, the area around Davao Global Township (Matina) or SM Lanang is another option.

Move between food bazaars and city restaurants to eat. August is durian season, so snacks such as durian ice cream and durian cake are easy to find. Many hotels do not allow durian because of its smell, so it is better to eat it outside. Carrying plenty of cash is handy at small stalls. If you like coffee, the cafes featured in the city's guide (such as Kapeweñoz and Purge Coffee Roaster) are worth a visit. At the food bazaars around the city you can casually try local dishes and grilled items.
Book flights and lodging early, from around July when the official schedule is released.
The parade starts early in the morning, so it is safer to stay in the city the day before.
Keep your bag to a small pouch, and bring a clear water bottle, a hat and comfortable shoes.
Bring plenty of cash. Many small stalls do not accept cards.
Ask permission before taking close-up photos of performers in traditional costume.
Get on and off Grab or taxis outside the closed area.
Schedules and venues change every year. In 2026 the showdown venue moved to the Coastal Road for the first time, so check the latest announcements.
During Kadayawan, city malls often hold large food bazaars, which are good places to rest and eat out of the heat.
Buying crafts at the traditional houses directly from the community is the best way to support them. Ask the price before buying and bargain fairly.
The parade route is closed to traffic and very crowded, so check bag inspections and the prohibited items list in advance.

In 2026 the city government announced a ban at all Kadayawan events on firearms, knives, alcohol, backpacks, umbrellas, lighters, toy guns, laser pointers, non-transparent water containers and jackets or hoodies, while police urged visitors to avoid bulky backpacks and oversized bags. This may change from year to year, so check the latest announcement.
Watch out for pickpockets and lost phones, and keep valuables in front of you.
It is very hot at midday and rain can come suddenly, so drink water often.
Check travel safety information for the Mindanao region (such as travel advisories) before you leave.
Even when venues change, announcements from the city tourism office are the most accurate.
The center of the festival. It is a good base for combining sightseeing with food.
Davao's main cathedral, close to San Pedro Square, where the grand parade ends.
A highland park reached by road from the city; travel time depends on traffic, so check locally. It is a pleasant, cool place to rest away from the midday heat.
An island across the water from the city by boat, good for a rest at the beach.
